title: Connect Your Agents
lede: Each agent connects its own way. Pick one and follow its steps. Aide runs the agent on the computer where it is installed, and you give it tasks from here, from your phone, or through your assistants.
machineNote: The computer that runs the agent. The agent must be installed there.
noMachine: No computer of yours is online. Open Aide on the computer that runs your agents, or turn on sharing this computer’s agents in Settings › Machines.

state.offline: {{machine}} is offline: Aide can’t check it now.
state.signIn: Found on {{machine}}, but not signed in
state.unconfirmed: Detected on {{machine}}, sign-in unconfirmed (run a test task below to verify automatically)
state.appOnly: Only the {{app}} app is on {{machine}}, not the part Aide runs
state.broken: Found on {{machine}}, but it fails to start
state.noAnswer: Found on {{machine}}, but it didn’t answer the check
state.signInClaude: Claude Code's command line is on {{machine}}, but not signed in (the Claude desktop app's sign-in does not carry over)
state.signInSeen: Found on {{machine}}; when it last ran in Aide ({{when}}) it said it isn’t signed in

fix.checkAgain: Then click Check Again. Aide looks for it every time you do; there is no need to restart anything.
fix.offline: Open Aide on {{machine}}, or wake it up. Its status comes back as soon as it is online.
fix.customMissing: Check the command: is the program installed on {{machine}}, under that name or at that full path? Edit the agent below and click Test Connection to see what happens.
fix.retest: First check whether it really isn’t signed in: click Run Test below. If it runs, it shows as signed in; if it still says it isn’t, sign in as the next step says.

project.none: A test task runs in a project: {{agent}} has none on {{machine}} yet (a folder it may work in). Add one first.

test.runNote: Asks the agent one short question in an empty folder. Nothing in your projects changes.
test.startNote: Starts a real task in your project “{{project}}”: the agent says hello and changes nothing. It opens in Aide, like any task.
test.prompt: This is a test from Aide. Reply with one short sentence: say hello and name the folder you are working in. Do not change any files.
test.started: Test task started. It shows in Aide’s task list.
test.notLoggedIn: Didn't work: Claude Code's command line is not signed in. The desktop app's sign-in doesn't carry over, so tasks for Claude fail on this machine.
test.notReady: Test {{agent}} here once it can be used on {{machine}}: first do what Status above says.

deepseek.intro: DSH is a coding agent (a desktop app that works with your DeepSeek account or API key). Aide runs the DSH installed on your computer: the one in the desktop app, or the dsh command.
deepseek.need1: DSH installed on the computer that runs it: the DSH desktop app (installed anywhere), or the dsh command.
deepseek.need2: DSH set up with your DeepSeek account or API key: open DSH once and send it a message to be sure it answers.
deepseek.need3: Aide open on that computer and signed in to your account (this computer already is).
deepseek.step1: Choose the computer that runs DSH above (this one is chosen for you).
deepseek.step2: Look at Status: it should say “Detected”. If it doesn’t, follow the list under it, then click Check Again.
deepseek.step3: If DSH has no project yet, click Add Project… and choose a folder it may work in.
deepseek.step4: Click Run Test. DSH answers one short question.
deepseek.step5: Click Start Test Task. A real task starts and opens in Aide.
deepseek.fixInstall: Is DSH installed on {{machine}}? Install the DSH desktop app or the dsh command, and open it once.
deepseek.fixWhere: Installed and still not found? Aide finds the DSH app where Windows says it is: in its list of installed programs, and the DSH running now. Open DSH once, then check again here. The dsh command counts only if a new terminal finds it (type dsh --version there).
deepseek.fixAppOnly: The DSH app is there, but the dsh it carries isn’t found in it. Update DSH, open it once, then check again here. If it still isn’t found, install the dsh command (npm install -g @deepseek-ai/dsh), or add it under Other Agent by dsh’s full path.
deepseek.fixSignIn: Open DSH and sign in or set up your DeepSeek API key there.
deepseek.testFailedHint: If the reason mentions a key, an account or a sign-in, open DSH, set up your DeepSeek account or API key there, and run the test again.
deepseek.where1: Tasks you start in Aide with DSH are in Aide’s task list, on every device of yours.
deepseek.where2: DSH’s own sessions (the ones you open in DSH, or another tool does) are on the DSH Sessions page in Aide’s sidebar, read only.
deepseek.where3: DSH also saves each task Aide starts in its own session history on that computer, next to yours. DSH Desktop may not list them: each task works in its own copy of the project folder that Aide makes.

claude.intro: Claude here is Claude Desktop, Anthropic’s desktop app. Aide runs the Claude Code that Claude Desktop uses on its Code tab: nothing else to install.
claude.need1: Claude Desktop installed and signed in to your Claude account (or Claude Code installed on its own).
claude.need2: Open Claude Desktop’s Code tab once and start a short session there. That downloads Claude Code, which Aide runs.
claude.need3: Claude Code signed in, with a Claude plan or an API key: if it answers on the Code tab, it is.
claude.step1: Choose the computer that has Claude Desktop above (this one is chosen for you).
claude.step2: Look at Status: it should say “Detected”. If it doesn’t, follow the list under it, then click Check Again.
claude.step3: If Claude Code has no project yet, click Add Project… and choose a folder it may work in.
claude.step4: Click Run Test. Claude Code answers one short question.
claude.step5: Click Start Test Task. A real task starts and opens in Aide.
claude.fixInstall: Install Claude Desktop from claude.ai/download and sign in (or install Claude Code on its own).
claude.fixWhere: Have Claude Desktop already? Open its Code tab once and start a short session: the app downloads Claude Code only then.
claude.fixCodeTab: Claude Desktop hasn’t downloaded Claude Code yet. Open Claude Desktop, sign in, open its Code tab and start a short session there.
claude.fixSignIn: Tasks Aide hands out run with the Claude Code command line, which needs its own sign-in once; the Claude desktop app being signed in doesn't count. Use “Sign in on …” under Connection details below: it gives a sign-in address you open on any device; sign in and enter the code back in Aide, no terminal needed.
claude.testFailedHint: If it says “Not logged in”, Claude Code's command line is not signed in (whether the desktop app is doesn't matter): see Status above.
claude.where1: Tasks you start in Aide with Claude are in Aide’s task list, on every device of yours.
claude.where2: Claude Desktop lists them too, on its Code tab, after it restarts, once you have opened a session there yourself. The Microsoft Store version of Claude Desktop doesn’t.
claude.where3: Continue one in Claude Desktop only once Aide is done with it: its title ends with who started it “via Aide”.
claude.assistant: Want Claude Desktop’s chat to give tasks to your agents instead? That is a different connection: Claude under Assistants, above.

codex.intro: Codex is OpenAI’s coding agent. Aide runs the codex command installed on your computer.
codex.need1: The Codex command-line tool installed on the computer that runs it (OpenAI’s instructions: npm install -g @openai/codex).
codex.need2: Codex signed in: run codex login once in a terminal.
codex.step1: Choose the computer that has Codex above (this one is chosen for you).
codex.step2: Look at Status: it should say “Detected”. If it doesn’t, follow the list under it, then click Check Again.
codex.step3: If Codex has no project yet, click Add Project… and choose a folder it may work in.
codex.step4: Click Run Test. Codex answers one short question.
codex.step5: Click Start Test Task. A real task starts and opens in Aide.
codex.fixInstall: Install the Codex command-line tool on {{machine}} (npm install -g @openai/codex). The ChatGPT or Codex app alone isn’t enough.
codex.fixWhere: Installed already? Open a new terminal and type codex --version: Aide finds Codex where a new terminal does.
codex.fixSignIn: Sign Codex in once: open a terminal (PowerShell on Windows), paste the command below and press Enter.
codex.testFailedHint: If the reason says it isn’t logged in, sign Codex in (see Status above) and run the test again.
codex.where1: Tasks you start in Aide with Codex are in Aide’s task list, on every device of yours.

antigravity.intro: Antigravity is Google’s first-class coding agent, running on your computer via its official ACP server with three-tier permission presets (Read only / Workspace write / Full access) and live session model discovery.
antigravity.step1: Choose the computer that has Antigravity above (this one is chosen for you).
antigravity.step2: Look at Status: it should say “Detected”. If it doesn’t, follow the list under it, then click Check Again.
antigravity.step3: If Antigravity has no project yet, click Add Project… and choose a folder it may work in.
antigravity.step4: Click Run Test. Antigravity answers one short question.
antigravity.step5: Click Start Test Task. A real task starts and opens in Aide.
antigravity.fixInstall: Click Install Antigravity ACP Server above: the Antigravity desktop app doesn’t bring this server, and Aide installs it for you.
antigravity.fixWhere: Rather install it yourself? Unpack the official release into ~/.local/share/antigravity-acp/ (%LOCALAPPDATA%\antigravity-acp\ on Windows), or put agy_acp_server on a new terminal’s PATH.
antigravity.fixSignIn: Sign Antigravity in once: open a terminal (PowerShell on Windows), paste the command below and follow the sign-in link.
antigravity.testFailedHint: If the reason says it isn’t logged in, run aide agent login antigravity (see Status above) and run the test again.
antigravity.where1: Tasks you start in Aide with Antigravity are in Aide’s task list on every device, with machine/project selection, three-tier permission presets, and full conversation continuation.
antigravity.needServer: Google’s official Antigravity ACP server (agy_acp_server): it is what Aide runs, not the Antigravity desktop app.
antigravity.needServerMissing: {{machine}} doesn’t have Google’s official Antigravity ACP server yet (the desktop app doesn’t bring it): click Install Antigravity ACP Server under Status below, and Aide installs it.
antigravity.needServerBroken: The Antigravity ACP server on {{machine}} doesn’t run: see why under Status below; Install Antigravity ACP Server installs it again.
antigravity.needServerOk: Google’s official Antigravity ACP server is installed on {{machine}}.
antigravity.needSignIn: Your Google account’s sign-in: only you can give it, in a browser; Aide can’t do it for you.
antigravity.needSignInMissing: Not signed in yet, which only you can do: run aide agent login antigravity once in a terminal, and allow it with your Google account in the browser that opens.
antigravity.needSignInUnconfirmed: Whether it is signed in shows once it runs: if you already signed in inside the Antigravity app, you don’t need to sign in again — click Start Test Task (or Run Test) below, and once it runs it shows as signed in. Only if it answers that it isn’t, run aide agent login antigravity once in a terminal and allow it with your Google account.
antigravity.needSignInOk: Signed in with your Google account.
antigravity.needSignInLater: Sign in once the server is installed, which only you can do: run aide agent login antigravity once in a terminal and allow it with your Google account.
antigravity.installWhat: Aide downloads the Antigravity ACP server from Google’s official releases, checks it against the official ACP registry’s SHA-256, installs it on {{machine}} where Aide looks for it, and checks again.
antigravity.needSignInSeen: When it last ran in Aide it said it isn’t signed in. The Antigravity ACP server keeps its sign-in apart from the Antigravity app’s, so signing in to the app may not carry over: click Run Test below to check again; if it still says it isn’t, run aide agent login antigravity once in a terminal and allow it with your Google account.

custom.intro: Connect any coding agent Aide doesn’t list, if it speaks the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). Tell Aide how to start it; Aide keeps it on that computer and lists it with the others. An agent without ACP that can run commands in a terminal connects under Assistants below, as Other Agent.
custom.need1: The agent installed on the computer that runs it, and its own sign-in or key ready.
custom.need2: The command that starts it in ACP mode, from its documentation (often an --acp argument).
custom.step1: Choose the computer that runs the agent above.
custom.step2: Fill in the form. Each field says what goes there, with an example.
custom.step3: Click Test Connection: Aide starts the agent once and checks that it answers. If it doesn’t, it says why.
custom.step4: Click Save. The agent is listed with the others at once, and its tasks start like theirs.
custom.step5: Then Run Test and Start Test Task, as for the other agents.
custom.removeMessage: It is taken off {{machine}}, with the keys saved for it. A task of it that is running goes on; no new task starts with it.
custom.name: Name
custom.nameHelp: How Aide and your assistants call it: lower-case letters, digits and -. It can’t be changed later.
custom.commandHelp: The program that starts this agent: a command a new terminal on that computer finds, or its full path. On Windows, given just a command’s name, Aide also looks for it in the list of installed programs and among the programs running.
custom.argsHelp: What follows the command, separated by spaces; put quotes around one that has spaces. They must start the agent in ACP mode.
custom.envHelp: Added to the agent’s environment. Names like …KEY, …TOKEN or …PASSWORD are secret: they are kept in that computer’s credential store (on Windows, encrypted for your user), never in its settings file, and never shown again.
custom.dirHelp: Usually empty: the agent starts in the task’s project folder. Fill it in only if the agent must start in a folder of its own.
custom.testOk: Connected: {{agent}} answered and opened a session.
custom.testOkAs: Connected: it says it is {{title}} {{version}}, and opened a session.
custom.testAuth: It asks to sign in first ({{methods}}). Sign in with the agent’s own tool on that computer, or give its key above, then test again.
custom.update: Update Aide on {{machine}} to add agents there.
custom.registryNote: From agentclientprotocol/registry: installed per machine. A binary package is installed only when the Registry declares its SHA-256, and must match it; otherwise its npx/uvx package is used, or it cannot be installed. Sign-in and credentials stay with the agent.
custom.registrySearch: Filter official ACP agents (e.g. opencode, gemini, claude)…
custom.registryInstalledToast: Installed “{{name}}” from the official ACP Registry on {{machine}}
custom.registryFallback: Could not refresh remote registry; showing {{source}} catalog ({{reason}}).

problem.name: Give it a name: lower-case letters, digits and -, starting with a letter.
problem.builtIn: Aide already has an agent by that name. Choose another.
problem.command: Give the command that starts the agent.
problem.envName: A variable name has letters, digits and _ only, and doesn’t start with a digit.
problem.envValue: Give the secret variable a value.

assistants.intro: Assistants such as Muse, Grok Bot, ChatGPT, Claude Desktop’s chat or OpenClaw don’t run on your computer: they give tasks to the coding agents above. One logs in with your Aide account and password, and is ready at once: there’s nothing for you to approve. One not listed connects as Other Agent if it can run commands in a terminal (WorkBuddy, for one): it installs the Aide command line and logs in with the account and password.
assistants.name: Name

steps.claude: In Claude Desktop, open Settings › Connectors, click Add custom connector, and paste the address below.
steps.chatgpt: In ChatGPT, open Settings › Connectors, turn on developer mode under Advanced, then click Create and put the address below in MCP server URL.

assistants.mcp2: {{app}} opens your Aide server’s login page: enter your Aide account and password, and click Connect.
assistants.mcp3: Once connected, it shows here and in Settings › Access. Confirm both pieces are wired — an open MCP session with periodic ping (keepalive) plus platform-appropriate inbox watching (daemon cron, message_wake webhook, or external poll hook) — then verify with a real message from the Aide app.
assistants.cli1: Copy the message below, replace {{password}} in it with your Aide password, and send it to {{name}}.
assistants.cli2: {{name}} installs the Aide command line as the message says, logs in, and declares its inbox-watching mechanism: nothing for you to approve, no code to compare.
assistants.cli3: Once logged in, it shows here and in Settings › Access. Finish by sending a real message from the Aide app and verifying it picks up and replies without reminders elsewhere.
assistants.mcpOlder: Aide on your server is older and doesn’t give an MCP address yet, so there’s no address to paste here. Update the server first: the address then shows here by itself. Or connect this assistant with the command line instead (choose Other Agent).
assistants.mcpOff: Your server gives no MCP address, so there’s no address to paste here: MCP is off on the server (start it with AIDE_RELAY_MCP=1). If the server is an older version, update it first too. Once that’s done, the address shows here by itself. Or connect this assistant with the command line instead (choose Other Agent).
assistants.mcpOffline: Not connected to your server yet: the address to paste shows here once it is.
assistants.password: Anyone with your password can log in to your account and run tasks on your computers. Send it only to assistants you trust; to stop one, sign it out in Settings › Access, or change the password (which signs out every assistant).
assistants.connectedBody: It is authorized for your projects. Showing online alone is not done: verify both keepalive and inbox watching (daemon cron, message_wake webhook, or external poll hook), and confirm it picks up and replies to a real message from the Aide app.
